files.text:
In February 1787 William Curtis, an apothecary who kept a botanic garden in the marshes at Lambeth, put out the first number of The Botanical Magazine: three plates of flowers and a page of text about each, stitched in a paper wrapper, for a shilling. His great work, the Flora Londinensis, had been admired and had lost him money. The magazine sold three thousand copies a month, and it was said of the two that one had brought him praise and the other pudding.

Every plate began as a drawing from a living plant, most of them in the first years by Sydenham Edwards, who was nineteen when his first was published and drew more than seventeen hundred in the next twenty-seven. The drawing was etched and engraved on a small copper plate, by Edwards himself at first and from 1792 by Francis Sansom, and printed in black on octavo sheets. Then each one had to be coloured. Three plates in three thousand copies is nine thousand sheets of watercolour a month, every one of them laid in by hand.

The colouring was done by a team, at one time some thirty of them, sitting side by side, many of them young women, some working in their own rooms and bringing the sheets back by the bundle. Each copied a pattern plate, one impression coloured as the artist meant it, kept on the table and followed sheet by sheet: the greens first, then the flower, then its small bright parts, a flat wash brought up to the engraved line and left to dry before the next went down beside it. They were paid by the piece, not by the hour, and not well, and the copies show it. Set two of the same plate side by side and one rose is pinker, one leaf a cooler green; here a wash has run over a stem, there a petal was missed and touched in afterwards.

The magazine outlived Curtis and every one of his artists. From 1834 Walter Hood Fitch, a calico designer’s apprentice from Glasgow, drew for it for more than forty years, some two thousand seven hundred plates, and drew them straight on the lithographic stone, which had taken over from copper by 1845. The prints were still coloured by hand, by colourists working from his patterns, for another century. It stopped only in 1948, when there were no longer enough people left who would do it, and the plates began to be printed in colour.

# florilegium A colourist's bench. Seven plates from *The Botanical Magazine* (Curtis, 1787-1791: passion flower, camellia, fuchsia, iris, moss rose, Jacobean lily, oriental poppy) come up one after another as bare impressions, black line on the magazine's cream paper, and are coloured by hand as you scroll. Each plate gets its greens first, then the flower, then the flower's small bright parts. A wash spreads as a wet front from where the brush went down, held back by the engraved lines. It is darker and faintly glossy while wet, and it dries from the edges in, with pigment drawn to the rim and settled into the paper's tooth, into exactly the real coloured plate. On a wide screen the pattern plate, the coloured model being copied, lies small beside the bench. A finished plate is laid aside on the pile and the next bare sheet is underneath. At the end the whole set lies on the bench together. The first plate is coloured slowly and in full, and the later ones a little faster, like work going on. Scroll back and it all un-colours. ```html
``` Or `import { florilegium } from './florilegium.js'` and call `florilegium(section, { src, mode, first, later, pattern })`; it returns `destroy()`. ## Options | attribute | option | default | what it does | |----------------|-----------|----------|--------------| | `data-src` | `src` | required | The collection JSON: per plate its id, size and washes in painting order. Beside it, per plate: `.webp` (the coloured scan), `-bare.webp` (the uncoloured impression), `-flat.webp` (each wash blurred inside its area: the pigment in suspension), `-map.webp` (lossless: wash index, arrival time, distance to the wash's edge, distance to a damp neighbour). | | `data-mode` | `mode` | `scroll` | `scroll`: a pinned bench on a runway. `static`: the finished set in a row. | | `data-first` | `first` | `110` | svh of scroll for the first plate. | | `data-later` | `later` | `52` | svh for each later plate. The runway is computed from these (about 560svh for seven plates). | | `data-pattern` | `pattern` | `on` | `off` hides the pattern plate. It only shows on wide screens. | Events (bubbling, for sound later): `florilegium:wash` with `detail: { plate, index, kind }` as each wash goes down while scrolling forward (kinds `leaf`, `stem`, `flower`, `detail`), `florilegium:plate` with `{ plate }` as a finished plate is laid aside, and `florilegium:done` when the set is complete. ## The real thing What the magazine's colourists did, and what a wash does on a printed sheet (Wilkinson, *A Treasure Regained*, Library of Congress Information Bulletin, 2003; Glasgow University Library on the magazine's history; Curtis, Anderson, Seims, Fleischer and Salesin, *Computer-Generated Watercolor*, SIGGRAPH 1997): - Each plate was printed in black from a small copper plate and coloured by hand by a team (at one time about thirty colourists, sitting side by side), copying a pattern plate coloured as the artist meant it. They were paid by the piece. Up to three thousand copies of each plate a month, coloured until 1948. - A colourist laid flat washes up to the engraved line, colour by colour: greens, the flower, then the small bright parts. The engraver's hatching does the shading, so a wash only has to give the colour. - The wet front advances unevenly and creeps along the lines. Wet paint is darker and glossy. As it dries, from the edges in, pigment gathers at the rim and settles into the tooth, and the wash ends lighter and matte. Where a wash meets one still damp there is a small bloom. Modelled: all of that, as transients that settle into each plate's own washes. Simplified: one wash per area (no glazing in layers, no gum arabic highlights laid separately). The order of washes inside a group climbs the plant from the bottom, which is not documented for these sheets. ## How it works **Offline (Python, scripts in the builder's scratch folder).** The pipeline is the one from `hand-colouring`, run per plate: 1. The scan (Missouri Botanical Garden's copy, via the Internet Archive) is cropped inside the page and white-balanced from its pink-yellow cast to an aged cream. 2. *Line from colour.* In linear light, the least-absorbed channel of each pixel against its local mean (and against its local ground for solid strokes) isolates the engraved line whatever wash lies over it. A clean smoothstep threshold makes an anti-aliased line mask, which is inked in fresh copperplate black-brown `#2a221c` on the plate's own paper (filled in under the washes from the paper around them). Away from the paint the bare image is the scan itself, so start and end agree there. Gutter shadow and foxing are kept out of the paint mask (components touching the scan's border, or far from the plant). 3. *Areas.* SLIC superpixels of the line-free colour layer, merged by colour on a region graph, folded, split into connected pieces, merged again across borders that are not engraved lines and into passages of neighbouring leaves or petals. Kinds come from hue (and a box round the flower where its colour is close to the leaves'). 4. *Arrival.* A brush path along each area's principal axis from its upper end; the front's arrival time is the geodesic travel time from the path, slowed on the engraved lines. 5. The map holds per pixel the wash index, arrival time, distance to the wash's edge and to a damp neighbour, lossless and exact. **In the browser.** One canvas covers the pinned bench and draws only the plate under the brush, with the `hand-colouring` shader, over a transparent ground, with its own sharp edge and shadow. The finished plates are the plain ``s of the markup, moved by `transform` onto the pile and into the set. The sheets waiting underneath are plain paper. A plate's textures are packed at the size shown, and the next plate's are packed while this one is being worked, so the change of plate never stalls. Each plate's schedule lives in its window of the scroll: one area after another, at most two or three wet at once, big areas 12-20svh on the first plate and about half that later. On a phone the sheet fills the width and a camera, a function of scroll only, zooms toward the wet washes and pulls back before the plate is laid aside. ## Theming | variable | default | used for | |-----------|-----------|----------| | `--paper` | `#f3f0e8` | the bench (the page) | | `--fl-runway` | set by the script | section height in scroll mode | ## Accessibility and motion - Without JS, or with reduced motion, the seven finished plates lie in a row (three to a row on a phone). They are ornament (`alt=""`); credits are in `assets/credits.json`. - Nothing is interactive, so a swipe always scrolls. ## Cost - Assets: 15 MB for seven plates, about 2.1 MB each (coloured, bare, flat, map), fetched as the bench reaches it: the next plate loads while the current one is coloured. - One full-screen quad, a dozen texture reads per pixel inside the sheet. A frame draws only while the scroll spring moves and the section is on screen. DPR capped at 2. WebGL2 for mipmaps (the phone's zoom); WebGL1 works without the zoom. ## Credits *The Botanical Magazine; or, Flower-Garden Displayed*, William Curtis, London, vols 1-4 (1787-1791), plates 28, 42, 47, 57, 69, 91, 97; hand-coloured engravings, drawn by Sydenham Edwards and others. Missouri Botanical Garden, Peter H. Raven Library, digitised for the Biodiversity Heritage Library (Internet Archive `mobot31753002719489`, `mobot31753002719497`). Public domain. The separations are ours. No third-party code.
